overview: The email validator checks one or more email addresses against a syntax rule and marks each line as valid or invalid. It reports the total, how many passed and how many failed, which makes it convenient for cleaning up a pasted list before an import.

The check follows the shape of a practical email address: a local part made of letters, digits and common special characters, an at sign, and a domain made of labels separated by dots. It rejects spaces, missing at signs and labels that begin or end with a hyphen. It is deliberately permissive about things that are technically legal, such as plus addressing and subdomains, because those are common in real use.

Syntax validation is not delivery validation. The tool cannot tell you whether a mailbox exists, whether the domain accepts mail, whether the address is a disposable one or whether the person wants to hear from you. For a mailing list, send a confirmation message; that is the only reliable proof that an address works and is controlled by its owner.
useCases: Spot typos in a list of addresses before importing contacts.
Check the format of an address collected in a form.
Separate malformed lines from plausible ones in a pasted CSV column.
Validate test fixtures without sending email.
Confirm that plus addressing is accepted by a form.
email-validator.workedExample: Paste four lines: jane.doe+news@example.co.uk, alex@sub.example.org, jane doe@example.com and jane@-example.com. The first two are marked Valid. The third is Invalid because it contains a space, and the fourth is Invalid because the domain label starts with a hyphen. The summary reports four addresses, two valid and two invalid, and the output keeps the original line next to each verdict.
limits: The rule checks syntax only. It cannot confirm that the domain exists, has a mail exchanger or accepts the mailbox.
A dotless domain such as jane@example is accepted because it is syntactically possible on private networks, even though it is not a usable public address.
Internationalised addresses with non-ASCII characters in the domain are not normalised or fully validated.
It does not detect disposable providers, role accounts, duplicates or addresses that have previously bounced.
email-validator.privacy: Validation happens entirely in your browser. Addresses are not uploaded, stored or checked against any external service.

faq.q: Does a valid result mean the email will arrive?
faq.a: No. It only means the text looks like an address. Delivery depends on the domain, the mailbox and the receiving server's filtering.

faq.q: Why is a dotless domain shown as valid?
faq.a: The syntax permits it for internal hosts. If you need public deliverability, require at least one dot in the domain as an extra check.

faq.q: Can I validate a whole list at once?
faq.a: Yes. Put one address per line and the tool checks each line separately and reports totals.

overview: The ISBN validator checks whether a 10- or 13-digit International Standard Book Number has a correct check digit. It removes spaces and hyphens, detects the format from the length, applies the appropriate checksum and reports whether the number is valid.

ISBN-13 uses a weighted sum in which alternating digits are multiplied by 1 and 3, and the final digit makes the total a multiple of 10. ISBN-10 uses weights from 10 down to 1, and the final character may be X to represent 10. A single mistyped digit almost always breaks the checksum, which is why the check digit is useful for catching transcription errors.

Passing the checksum does not prove that a book exists. The number could be a valid but unassigned identifier, or it could belong to a different edition than the one you expect. Use the result to catch typos, then look up the ISBN with a bookseller, library catalogue or national ISBN agency for publication details.
useCases: Check a handwritten ISBN before ordering a book.
Verify a list of ISBNs imported from a spreadsheet.
Distinguish an ISBN-10 from an ISBN-13 by length.
Catch a transposed digit in a citation.
Confirm that the X check digit in an old ISBN-10 is correct.
isbn-validator.workedExample: Enter 978-0-306-40615-7. After removing hyphens the value is 9780306406157, which has 13 digits. The weighted sum of the first 12 digits is 9 + 21 + 8 + 0 + 9 + 0 + 18 + 0 + 3 + 45 + 1 + 15 = 129; the check digit that brings the total to the next multiple of 10 is 7, which matches. Entering 978-0-306-40615-6 instead fails, because the final digit does not match the checksum.
limits: The tool validates the checksum only. It does not search a bibliographic database or confirm that the ISBN is assigned.
It does not convert between ISBN-10 and ISBN-13, which requires recalculating the check digit and, for some ranges, a prefix change.
Hyphens and spaces are ignored, but other separators and malformed groupings are not interpreted.
A valid checksum can still belong to a different edition, binding or format of a book.
isbn-validator.privacy: ISBNs are checked locally in your browser. No numbers are sent to ToolNova or retained.

faq.q: Can an ISBN-10 end in X?
faq.a: Yes. X represents the value 10 in the check position, for example 0-8044-2957-X. The validator accepts upper- or lowercase X.

faq.q: Why do I need to remove hyphens?
faq.a: You do not; the tool strips spaces and hyphens automatically. It only needs the digits and any final X.

faq.q: Does a valid ISBN prove the book exists?
faq.a: No. It proves the number is internally consistent. Confirm the title and edition with a catalogue or bookseller.

overview: The Luhn validator checks whether a number satisfies the Luhn checksum, the mod-10 formula used by most payment cards, IMEI numbers and some account identifiers. It also reports the digit count, the check digit and a rough prefix hint such as Visa-like or Mastercard-like.

The algorithm starts from the rightmost digit, doubles every second digit, subtracts 9 from any result above 9, and adds everything together. If the total is a multiple of 10, the number passes. Because the check digit is part of the calculation, changing any single digit or swapping two adjacent digits almost always causes a failure, which makes the check useful for catching typing mistakes.

A passing checksum does not mean a card is valid, active or chargeable. It only means the digits are internally consistent. Anyone can invent a number that passes the Luhn check, and the prefix hint is a pattern match rather than an issuer lookup. Never enter a real card number into a website you do not control; use the published test numbers instead.
useCases: Check a test card number while building a payment form.
Catch a mistyped digit before submitting an account number.
Teach how the mod-10 checksum works with a worked example.
Verify that a sample IMEI passes its checksum.
Sanity-check a number copied from a document.
luhn-validator.workedExample: Check 4111 1111 1111 1111, a standard Visa test number. After removing spaces it has 16 digits. Doubling every second digit from the right and reducing values above nine produces a sum that is a multiple of 10, so the validator reports a valid checksum. Change the last digit to 2 and the sum is no longer divisible by 10, so 4111 1111 1111 1112 fails. The prefix hint for the valid number is "Visa-like", but that is only a pattern, not proof of an account.
limits: The Luhn check validates format only. It cannot confirm that a card exists, is active, has funds or belongs to the person entering it.
The prefix hint is a simple regular expression for common card networks and does not identify the issuer or card type reliably.
Numbers from 2 to 19 digits are accepted, so non-card identifiers that use Luhn can also be checked, but other lengths are rejected.
It does not perform expiry, CVV or address verification, and it must never be used as the only validation on a payment form.
luhn-validator.privacy: Validation runs locally in your browser and the number is not transmitted. Despite that, only paste real card details into systems you are authorised to use; prefer official test numbers for development.

faq.q: Does a Luhn pass mean the card is valid?
faq.a: No. It means the digits satisfy a checksum. Authorisation by the issuer is the only way to know whether a card can be charged.

faq.q: Why do some valid numbers fail?
faq.a: Not every identifier uses Luhn, and some cards or regional systems use different check rules. A failure is a strong hint of a typo, but context matters.

faq.q: Can I use this to validate an IMEI?
faq.a: Yes, IMEI numbers use the Luhn formula. Enter the 15 digits without spaces and check whether the checksum passes.
